concepts.name: Related rates
concepts.statement: If two related quantities are changing over time, the rates at which the quantities change are related: when a balloon is filled with air, dV/dt and dr/dt are related rates because the volume V is related to the radius r.

concepts.name: Solving a related-rates problem
concepts.statement: To solve a related-rates problem, assign symbols to all variables and draw a figure, state the information given and the rate to be determined, find an equation relating the variables, differentiate both sides with respect to the independent variable using the chain rule, and only then substitute the known values and solve for the unknown rate.

concepts.name: Linear approximation
concepts.statement: For a function f differentiable at a, the linear function L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a), whose graph is the tangent line to f at a, is the linear approximation of f at x = a, also called the tangent line approximation or linearization of f at a; for x near a, f(x) ≈ L(x).

concepts.name: Differential
concepts.statement: For a differentiable function y = f(x), the differential dx is an independent variable that can be assigned any nonzero real number, and the differential dy is defined to be dy = f′(x)dx; the equation dy = f′(x)dx is the differential form of the derivative of y with respect to x.

concepts.name: Approximating change with differentials
concepts.statement: If x changes from a to a + dx, the differential dy = f′(a)dx, the change in y along the tangent line, approximates the actual change Δy = f(a + dx) − f(a) in y, and the approximation is better the closer dx is to zero.

concepts.name: Propagated error
concepts.statement: The propagated error is the error in a calculated quantity f(x) that results from a measurement error dx in x; it can be estimated by dy ≈ f′(x)dx.

concepts.name: Relative error
concepts.statement: Given an absolute error Δq for a particular quantity q, the relative error is Δq/q, the error as a fraction of the quantity.

concepts.name: Percentage error
concepts.statement: The percentage error is the relative error expressed as a percentage, 100 Δq/q.

concepts.name: Absolute extremum
concepts.statement: Let f be a function defined over an interval I and c ∈ I. f has an absolute maximum on I at c if f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x ∈ I, and an absolute minimum on I at c if f(c) ≤ f(x) for all x ∈ I; either one is an absolute extremum on I at c.

concepts.name: Extreme Value Theorem
concepts.statement: If f is a continuous function over the closed, bounded interval [a, b], then there is a point in [a, b] at which f has an absolute maximum over [a, b] and a point in [a, b] at which f has an absolute minimum over [a, b].

concepts.name: Local extremum
concepts.statement: A function f has a local maximum at c if there is an open interval I containing c, contained in the domain of f, with f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x ∈ I, and a local minimum at c if f(c) ≤ f(x) for all x ∈ I; either one is a local extremum at c.

concepts.name: Critical point
concepts.statement: Let c be an interior point in the domain of f. c is a critical number of f if f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) is undefined, and the point (c, f(c)) is a critical point of f; the two terms are often used interchangeably.

concepts.name: Fermat’s theorem
concepts.statement: If f has a local extremum at c and f is differentiable at c, then f′(c) = 0: a local extremum occurs at a critical point.

concepts.name: Location of absolute extrema
concepts.statement: Let f be a continuous function over a closed, bounded interval I. The absolute maximum and the absolute minimum of f over I must occur at endpoints of I or at critical points of f in I.

concepts.name: Locating absolute extrema over a closed interval
concepts.statement: For a continuous function f over [a, b], evaluate f at the endpoints a and b, find the critical points of f in (a, b) and evaluate f there, and compare: the largest value is the absolute maximum of f and the smallest the absolute minimum.

concepts.name: Rolle’s theorem
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over the closed interval [a, b] and differentiable over the open interval (a, b) with f(a) = f(b). Then there exists at least one c ∈ (a, b) such that f′(c) = 0.

concepts.name: Mean Value Theorem
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over [a, b] and differentiable over (a, b). Then there exists at least one point c ∈ (a, b) at which the slope of the tangent line equals the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)): f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).

concepts.name: Functions with a derivative of zero
concepts.statement: Let f be differentiable over an interval I. If f′(x) = 0 for all x ∈ I, then f(x) is constant for all x ∈ I.

concepts.name: Constant difference theorem
concepts.statement: If f and g are differentiable over an interval I and f′(x) = g′(x) for all x ∈ I, then f(x) = g(x) + C for some constant C.

concepts.name: Increasing and decreasing functions corollary
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over [a, b] and differentiable over (a, b). If f′(x) > 0 for all x ∈ (a, b), then f is an increasing function over [a, b]; if f′(x) < 0 for all x ∈ (a, b), then f is a decreasing function over [a, b].

concepts.name: First derivative test
concepts.statement: Suppose f is continuous over an interval I containing a critical point c and differentiable over I except possibly at c. If f′ changes sign from positive to negative as x increases through c, f(c) is a local maximum of f; if from negative to positive, f(c) is a local minimum; if f′ has the same sign on both sides of c, f(c) is neither.

concepts.name: Using the first derivative test
concepts.statement: To find the local extrema of a function f continuous over an interval I, divide I at the critical points of f (and at any point where f′ is discontinuous), find the sign of f′ in each subinterval from a test point, and read from the first derivative test whether f has a local maximum, a local minimum or neither at each critical point.

concepts.name: Concavity
concepts.statement: Let f be differentiable over an open interval I. If f′ is increasing over I, f is concave up over I; if f′ is decreasing over I, f is concave down over I. Concavity is the upward or downward curve of the graph of a function.

concepts.name: Test for concavity
concepts.statement: Let f be twice differentiable over an interval I. If f″(x) > 0 for all x ∈ I, then f is concave up over I; if f″(x) < 0 for all x ∈ I, then f is concave down over I.

concepts.name: Inflection point
concepts.statement: If f is continuous at a and f changes concavity at a, the point (a, f(a)) is an inflection point of f.

concepts.name: Second derivative test
concepts.statement: Suppose f′(c) = 0 and f″ is continuous over an interval containing c. If f″(c) > 0, f has a local minimum at c; if f″(c) < 0, f has a local maximum at c; if f″(c) = 0, the test is inconclusive.

concepts.name: Limit at infinity
concepts.statement: If the values of f(x) become arbitrarily close to L as x becomes sufficiently large, f has a limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L; if they become arbitrarily close to L for x < 0 as |x| becomes sufficiently large, f has a limit at negative infinity, lim_{x→−∞} f(x) = L.

concepts.name: Horizontal asymptote
concepts.statement: If lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L or lim_{x→−∞} f(x) = L, the line y = L is a horizontal asymptote of f; unlike a vertical asymptote, a horizontal asymptote may be crossed, even an unlimited number of times.

concepts.name: Infinite limit at infinity
concepts.statement: A function f has an infinite limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = ∞, if f(x) becomes arbitrarily large for x sufficiently large, and a negative infinite limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = −∞, if f(x) < 0 and |f(x)| becomes arbitrarily large for x sufficiently large; limits as x → −∞ are defined in the same way.

concepts.name: Formal definition of a limit at infinity
concepts.statement: A function f has a limit at infinity if there exists a real number L such that for all ε > 0 there exists N > 0 with |f(x) − L| < ε for all x > N; then lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L. A limit at negative infinity asks for N < 0 and all x < N.

concepts.name: Formal definition of an infinite limit at infinity
concepts.statement: A function f has an infinite limit at infinity, lim_{x→∞} f(x) = ∞, if for all M > 0 there exists an N > 0 such that f(x) > M for all x > N; it has a negative infinite limit at infinity if for all M < 0 there exists N > 0 with f(x) < M for all x > N.

concepts.name: End behavior of rational functions
concepts.statement: For a rational function f(x) = p(x)/q(x), the end behavior is decided by the degrees of p and q: if the degree of p is less than the degree of q, y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote; if they are equal, y = aₙ/bₙ, the ratio of the leading coefficients, is a horizontal asymptote; if the degree of p is greater, f(x) approaches ∞ or −∞ at each end.

concepts.name: Oblique asymptote
concepts.statement: The line y = mx + b is an oblique asymptote of f if f(x) approaches it as x → ∞ or x → −∞; a rational function whose numerator has degree one more than its denominator has one, found by long division.

concepts.name: End behavior of transcendental functions
concepts.statement: sin x and cos x oscillate between −1 and 1 and tan x does not approach a limit or ±∞ as x → ±∞; eˣ approaches ∞ as x → ∞ and 0 as x → −∞, and ln x approaches ∞ as x → ∞.

concepts.name: Drawing the graph of a function
concepts.statement: To sketch the graph of f, determine its domain, its x- and y-intercepts, its end behavior from the limits at ±∞ (a horizontal or an oblique asymptote) and its vertical asymptotes, then find from f′ where f increases and decreases and its local extrema, and from f″ where it is concave up or down and its inflection points.

concepts.name: Optimization problem
concepts.statement: An optimization problem is a problem that is solved by finding the maximum or minimum value of a function, such as maximizing an area or a revenue or minimizing a cost, a time or a surface area.

concepts.name: Solving optimization problems
concepts.statement: To solve an optimization problem, introduce the variables and draw a figure, decide which quantity is to be maximized or minimized, write it as a function of one variable using the equations relating the variables, find the domain the physical problem allows, and locate its maximum or minimum from the critical points and the endpoints, or from the behavior of the function where the interval is open or unbounded.

concepts.name: L’Hôpital’s rule (0/0 case)
concepts.statement: Suppose f and g are differentiable over an open interval containing a, except possibly at a. If lim_{x→a} f(x) = 0 and lim_{x→a} g(x) = 0, then lim_{x→a} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{x→a} f′(x)/g′(x), assuming the limit on the right exists or is ∞ or −∞; it also holds for one-sided limits and for a = ±∞.

concepts.name: L’Hôpital’s rule (∞/∞ case)
concepts.statement: Suppose f and g are differentiable over an open interval containing a, except possibly at a, and lim_{x→a} f(x) and lim_{x→a} g(x) are each ∞ or −∞. Then lim_{x→a} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{x→a} f′(x)/g′(x), assuming the limit on the right exists or is ∞ or −∞; it also holds for a = ±∞ and for one-sided limits.

concepts.name: Indeterminate forms
concepts.statement: When evaluating a limit, the forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰ and 1^∞ are indeterminate: each has no meaning on its own, and further analysis is required to determine whether the limit exists and, if so, what its value is.

concepts.name: Evaluating indeterminate products and differences
concepts.statement: A limit of the form 0·∞ is rewritten as a quotient, f(x)g(x) = f(x)/(1/g(x)), and one of the form ∞ − ∞ is combined over a common denominator or otherwise rewritten, so that it takes the form 0/0 or ∞/∞ and L’Hôpital’s rule applies.

concepts.name: Evaluating indeterminate powers
concepts.statement: For a limit of f(x)^{g(x)} of the form 1^∞, ∞⁰ or 0⁰, take the natural logarithm, y = f(x)^{g(x)} giving ln y = g(x) ln f(x), find the limit of ln y as an indeterminate product, and since lim ln y = L gives lim y = e^L by continuity, the limit is e^L.

concepts.name: Growth rates of functions
concepts.statement: Suppose f and g approach infinity as x → ∞. g grows more rapidly than f as x → ∞ if lim_{x→∞} g(x)/f(x) = ∞, or equivalently lim_{x→∞} f(x)/g(x) = 0; if lim_{x→∞} f(x)/g(x) = M for some constant M ≠ 0, f and g grow at the same rate.

concepts.name: Growth of exponential and logarithmic functions
concepts.statement: The exponential function eˣ grows more rapidly than any power function xᵖ, p > 0, and the logarithmic function ln x grows more slowly than any power function xᵖ, p > 0, as x → ∞.

concepts.name: Newton’s method
concepts.statement: Newton’s method approximates a root of f(x) = 0: from an initial guess x₀ near the root, each approximation is the x-intercept of the tangent line to f at the one before, xₙ = xₙ₋₁ − f(xₙ₋₁)/f′(xₙ₋₁), and the numbers x₀, x₁, x₂, … typically approach the root.

concepts.name: Failures of Newton’s method
concepts.statement: Newton’s method fails when the list x₀, x₁, x₂, … does not approach a finite value or approaches a root other than the one sought: when f′(xₙ) = 0 for some n, when the initial guess is too far from the root, or when the approximations cycle between values.

concepts.name: Iterative process
concepts.statement: An iterative process generates a list of numbers x₀, x₁, x₂, x₃, … by starting with a number x₀ and defining xₙ = F(xₙ₋₁) for n ≥ 1 for some function F; Newton’s method is the iterative process with F(x) = x − f(x)/f′(x).

concepts.name: Cycles and chaos of an iterative process
concepts.statement: An iterative process may converge to a fixed point, bounce between values in a 2-cycle, 4-cycle or longer cycle, or behave chaotically, its values never settling and highly sensitive to the starting number; a cobweb diagram shows which.

concepts.name: Antiderivative
concepts.statement: A function F is an antiderivative of the function f if F′(x) = f(x) for all x in the domain of f; finding an antiderivative reverses differentiation.

concepts.name: General form of an antiderivative
concepts.statement: Let F be an antiderivative of f over an interval I. For each constant C, F(x) + C is also an antiderivative of f over I, and every antiderivative G of f over I is G(x) = F(x) + C for some constant C: the family of antiderivatives F(x) + C is the most general antiderivative of f.

concepts.name: Indefinite integral
concepts.statement: Given a function f, the indefinite integral of f, ∫f(x)dx, is the most general antiderivative of f: if F is an antiderivative of f, then ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C. f(x) is the integrand and x the variable of integration.

concepts.name: Power rule for integrals
concepts.statement: For n ≠ −1, ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C.

concepts.name: Properties of indefinite integrals
concepts.statement: Let F and G be antiderivatives of f and g and k any real number. Then ∫(f(x) ± g(x))dx = F(x) ± G(x) + C and ∫kf(x)dx = kF(x) + C: an indefinite integral of a sum, difference or constant multiple is found term by term.

concepts.name: Differential equation
concepts.statement: A differential equation is an equation that relates an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives; the solutions of dy/dx = f(x) are the antiderivatives of f.

concepts.name: Initial-value problem
concepts.statement: An initial-value problem asks for a function y that satisfies a differential equation dy/dx = f(x) together with an initial condition y(x₀) = y₀; it is solved by finding the family of antiderivatives of f and then the one that satisfies the initial condition.
